title: What Is RAG? Retrieval-Augmented Generation Explained
seoTitle: What Is RAG? Retrieval-Augmented Generation Explained
seoDescription: Learn how retrieval-augmented generation works, why RAG helps AI use external knowledge, and how production RAG systems are designed.
excerpt: Retrieval-augmented generation connects language models to external knowledge so answers can be grounded in information retrieved at request time.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: RAG retrieves relevant information before a language model generates its answer.
It can give models access to current, private or domain-specific knowledge without retraining the base model.
A production RAG system depends on retrieval quality, chunking, metadata, ranking and evaluation—not only the language model.
RAG can reduce unsupported answers, but it does not guarantee factual accuracy.
body: A language model knows patterns learned during training, but many useful applications need information that is newer, private or too specialized to live reliably inside model parameters. Retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG, addresses that problem by retrieving relevant material from an external knowledge source before asking the model to answer.

This changes the architecture of an AI application. Instead of treating the model as the entire knowledge system, RAG makes it one component in a pipeline that can search documents, databases or other repositories and place selected evidence into the model's context.

sections.heading: The basic RAG pipeline
paragraphs: A typical RAG system starts by preparing a knowledge base. Documents are cleaned and divided into smaller chunks. Those chunks can be represented as embeddings and stored with metadata in a search system or vector database.

When a user asks a question, the application converts the query into a representation suitable for retrieval, searches for relevant chunks and sends the strongest results to the language model together with the question. The model then generates an answer using that supplied context.
bullets: Index chunks for semantic, keyword or hybrid search.
Retrieve and rank evidence for each query.
Generate an answer using the selected evidence.

sections.heading: Why RAG is useful
paragraphs: The biggest advantage is separation between the model and the knowledge base. A company can update a product manual, policy or internal document and make the new information retrievable without training a new foundation model.

The same pattern can be used for public information. A research assistant can retrieve recent documents, while a support assistant can retrieve the latest product documentation. This is especially valuable when knowledge changes faster than model training cycles.

sections.heading: Embeddings and vector search
paragraphs: Embeddings are numerical representations designed to capture aspects of meaning. Text with related meaning can have nearby representations even when it does not use exactly the same words. Vector search uses this property to retrieve semantically related chunks.

Vector retrieval is not always enough. Exact identifiers, error codes and product names can work better with lexical search. Many mature systems therefore combine semantic and keyword retrieval and then rerank the candidates.

sections.heading: Chunking is an architectural decision
paragraphs: If chunks are too large, retrieval may return a long passage containing only a small amount of useful evidence. If chunks are too small, important context can be separated across several records. Good chunking often follows the structure of the source material rather than blindly splitting every fixed number of characters.
Metadata also matters. Product, date, access level, document type and section information can be used to filter retrieval before the model sees anything.

sections.heading: RAG does not eliminate hallucinations
paragraphs: Retrieving evidence improves grounding only when the evidence is relevant and the model uses it correctly. A system can retrieve the wrong document, miss an important passage or generate a claim that is not supported by the retrieved context.

Production applications therefore need evaluation. Teams can measure retrieval recall, ranking quality, answer correctness, citation quality and whether generated claims are supported by the provided evidence.

sections.heading: RAG, fine-tuning and long context
paragraphs: RAG and fine-tuning solve different problems. Fine-tuning is often useful for changing behavior, format or task performance. RAG is primarily a way to provide knowledge dynamically. They can be used together.

Large context windows also do not make retrieval irrelevant. Putting every available document into a prompt can be expensive and noisy. Retrieval helps select the information most likely to matter for a particular request.

sections.heading: Security in enterprise RAG
paragraphs: Connecting an AI assistant to private documents introduces authorization requirements. Retrieval must respect the user's permissions before content is placed into model context. A system that retrieves a confidential document for an unauthorized user has already failed even if the final answer does not quote it verbatim.

Organizations should also consider prompt injection inside retrieved documents, logging policies, sensitive-data handling and the security boundaries between the model, retrieval service and source systems.

faq.question: What does RAG stand for?
faq.answer: RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. It combines information retrieval with generative AI.

faq.question: Does RAG require a vector database?
faq.answer: No. Vector search is common, but RAG can use keyword search, relational databases, search engines, APIs or hybrid retrieval depending on the data and task.

faq.question: Is RAG better than fine-tuning?
faq.answer: They address different needs. RAG is useful for supplying changing or external knowledge, while fine-tuning is often used to alter model behavior or specialize task performance.
